puzzles.name: Thioredoxin redox active site
puzzles.blurb: The two cysteines here swap between a free dithiol and an internal disulfide, and that cycle is how thioredoxin hands reducing power to other proteins. The rigid Cys-Gly-Pro-Cys spacing holds the pair at exactly the distance a disulfide needs.

puzzles.name: P-loop, small GTPase
puzzles.blurb: This glycine-rich loop wraps the phosphates of bound GTP, and the glycines are there because anything with a side chain would collide with them. Mutations at the following residue, Gly12, lock Ras in its active state and are among the most common oncogenic changes in human cancer.

puzzles.name: CAAX prenylation box
puzzles.blurb: The very end of Ras, where a farnesyl lipid is attached to the cysteine so the protein can stick to the inner face of the membrane. Cut this tail off and Ras still binds GTP perfectly but can no longer signal, because it is floating in the cytosol.

puzzles.name: EF-hand calcium loop
puzzles.blurb: A twelve-residue loop whose aspartates and backbone carbonyls cage a single Ca2+ ion. Calmodulin carries four of these, and filling them swings the protein open to expose a hydrophobic groove that grabs its targets.

puzzles.name: Catalytic triad — histidine
puzzles.blurb: The histidine of the serine protease catalytic triad, which pulls a proton off the catalytic serine so it can attack the substrate. It sits far from the other two triad members in sequence and only meets them once the protein folds.

puzzles.name: Catalytic triad — aspartate
puzzles.blurb: The buried aspartate that orients the triad histidine and stabilises it once it picks up a proton. It never touches the substrate; it exists to make the histidine a better base.

puzzles.name: Catalytic triad — serine
puzzles.blurb: The nucleophilic serine that actually attacks the peptide bond, embedded in a Gly-Asp-Ser-Gly-Gly motif so conserved it is used to identify serine proteases from sequence alone. The flanking glycines leave the serine sterically exposed.

puzzles.name: Enterokinase activation site
puzzles.blurb: Four aspartates and a lysine mark where enterokinase cuts trypsinogen to switch on trypsin. The same sequence is used as an engineered cleavage tag precisely because so little else in a proteome looks like it.

puzzles.name: New N-terminus after activation
puzzles.blurb: The moment trypsinogen is cut, this isoleucine becomes a free N-terminus and buries itself in a pocket, snapping the active site into shape. Zymogen activation is a conformational switch triggered by a single new charge.

puzzles.name: Lysozyme catalytic glutamate
puzzles.blurb: Glu35 donates a proton to the glycosidic bond it is about to break, working as a general acid. Its unusually high pKa comes from sitting in a hydrophobic pocket, which is what keeps it protonated at working pH.

puzzles.name: Lysozyme catalytic aspartate
puzzles.blurb: Asp52 is the second half of lysozyme's catalytic pair, stabilising the positively charged intermediate that forms as the sugar ring is cleaved. It sits in a polar environment and stays deprotonated — the mirror image of Glu35 next door.

puzzles.name: Copper site, Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase
puzzles.blurb: Two of the histidines that hold the catalytic copper, which cycles between Cu(I) and Cu(II) to dismutate superoxide. SOD1 runs close to the diffusion limit, which makes it one of the fastest enzymes known.

puzzles.name: Transthyretin amyloid hotspot
puzzles.blurb: The valine here is position 30 of mature transthyretin, and its replacement by methionine is the most common cause of hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis. A single hydrophobic swap destabilises the tetramer enough for the monomers to misfold.

puzzles.name: Transthyretin N-terminus
puzzles.blurb: The start of mature transthyretin after its signal peptide is removed. Glycine and threonine make a flexible, polar N-terminal arm that stays disordered even in the crystal structures.

puzzles.name: Walker A motif
puzzles.blurb: The bacterial version of the phosphate-binding loop, doing the same job as the Ras P-loop with a different sequence. Comparing the two is a clean demonstration that structure is conserved far more tightly than sequence.

puzzles.name: Adenylate kinase LID hinge
puzzles.blurb: Part of the mobile LID domain that clamps shut over bound nucleotide during catalysis. Adenylate kinase is a textbook case of induced fit — the closed and open structures differ by around 30 angstroms.

puzzles.name: Zinc site, carbonic anhydrase II
puzzles.blurb: Two of the three histidines that hold the catalytic zinc, which lowers the pKa of a bound water molecule enough to strip a proton off it at neutral pH. The resulting hydroxide is what attacks CO2.

puzzles.name: Haemoglobin beta N-terminus
puzzles.blurb: Residue 6 of the beta chain is the glutamate that becomes valine in sickle cell disease. Swapping one charged residue for a hydrophobic one creates a sticky patch that lets deoxygenated haemoglobin polymerise into fibres.

puzzles.name: Proximal histidine region
puzzles.blurb: The proximal histidine bonds directly to the heme iron and is physically pulled when oxygen binds on the far side. That tug is transmitted through the helix and is the mechanical basis of cooperative oxygen binding.

puzzles.name: Haemoglobin alpha N-terminus
puzzles.blurb: The alpha chain begins differently from beta despite the two folding almost identically. Comparing the first few residues of each is a quick way to see how far two sequences can drift while keeping one shape.

puzzles.name: Insulin B chain N-terminus
puzzles.blurb: The start of the B chain, part of the surface that lets insulin monomers assemble into hexamers around zinc. Engineered changes in this region are what make fast-acting insulin analogues dissociate more quickly.

puzzles.name: Insulin A chain N-terminus
puzzles.blurb: The A chain begins here, immediately followed by the cysteines that disulfide-bond it to the B chain. Insulin is synthesised as a single chain and only becomes two once the connecting C-peptide is excised.

puzzles.name: Insulin intrachain disulfide
puzzles.blurb: Two adjacent cysteines, one bonding within the A chain and one reaching across to the B chain. Getting these pairings right is the hard part of producing insulin recombinantly.

puzzles.name: Ubiquitin N-terminus
puzzles.blurb: The opening strand of the beta-grasp fold, one of the most thermodynamically stable small domains known. Ubiquitin is so tolerant of heat and acid that boiling a lysate is a legitimate purification step.

puzzles.name: Ubiquitin Lys48
puzzles.blurb: Chains built through this lysine are the canonical signal for proteasomal degradation. Four linked ubiquitins is roughly the threshold the proteasome recognises.

puzzles.name: Ubiquitin Lys63
puzzles.blurb: Chains through Lys63 do not mean destruction — they signal in DNA repair and NF-kB activation. Same protein, same modification, different lysine, opposite outcome.

puzzles.name: Ubiquitin C-terminal tail
puzzles.blurb: The flexible tail whose terminal glycine forms an isopeptide bond to a target lysine. E1, E2 and E3 enzymes all handle this same five-residue tail.

puzzles.name: RGD integrin-binding motif
puzzles.blurb: The tripeptide integrins read when they grip the extracellular matrix, presented here on an exposed loop. RGD peptides are grafted onto biomaterials to persuade cells to adhere to them.

puzzles.name: Amyloid-beta aggregation core
puzzles.blurb: The central hydrophobic cluster of amyloid-beta, and the stretch that drives the peptide into cross-beta fibrils. Peptides copying this sequence were among the first designed aggregation inhibitors.

puzzles.name: HExxH zinc protease motif
puzzles.blurb: Two histidines separated by two arbitrary residues, both coordinating a catalytic zinc, with the glutamate activating the attacking water. The HExxH signature identifies metalloproteases across otherwise unrelated families.

puzzles.name: SV40 classical NLS
puzzles.blurb: A dense run of positive charge that importin-alpha reads as an instruction to carry the protein into the nucleus. It was the first nuclear localisation signal identified and is still the standard one to bolt onto engineered proteins.

puzzles.name: Polyhistidine tag
puzzles.blurb: Histidines chelate immobilised nickel, which is the entire basis of IMAC purification. The imidazole ring is the only side chain in the standard twenty that coordinates a divalent metal well at neutral pH.

puzzles.name: FLAG tag
puzzles.blurb: A short, highly charged epitope tag, deliberately hydrophilic so it stays on the protein surface and rarely disturbs folding. Its charge is also why FLAG-tagged proteins elute under mild conditions.

puzzles.name: Strep-tag II
puzzles.blurb: Binds engineered streptavidin, and is competed off with biotin analogues under conditions gentle enough to keep complexes intact. The tryptophan does most of the binding work.

puzzles.name: Myc epitope tag
puzzles.blurb: A linear epitope from the c-Myc protein, used because a well-characterised monoclonal antibody recognises it reliably. Linear epitopes are preferred as tags because they do not require a folded context.

puzzles.name: HA epitope tag
puzzles.blurb: Taken from influenza haemagglutinin, and one of the smallest tags that still gives clean immunodetection. Its tyrosines make it easy to detect but also slightly more perturbing than FLAG.

puzzles.name: TEV protease site
puzzles.blurb: Tobacco etch virus protease cuts after the glutamine, leaving almost no scar on the released protein. This is how an affinity tag is removed after it has done its job on the column.

puzzles.name: Thrombin cleavage site
puzzles.blurb: Thrombin cuts between the arginine and glycine, an older workhorse for tag removal. It is less specific than TEV, which is why internal cleavage of the target protein is a real risk.

puzzles.name: Sortase A recognition motif
puzzles.blurb: Sortase cuts between threonine and glycine and ligates the remainder to an incoming polyglycine, making it a protein-ligation tool rather than just a protease. Bacteria use it to staple surface proteins to cell wall peptidoglycan.

puzzles.name: Caspase-3 cleavage site
puzzles.blurb: Caspase-3 cuts after the second aspartate, and this sequence is the basis of most apoptosis assays. Caspases are unusual among proteases in demanding an aspartate at the cut site.

puzzles.name: Factor Xa cleavage site
puzzles.blurb: Factor Xa cuts after the arginine, leaving no extra residues on the protein's new N-terminus. It comes from the blood clotting cascade, where this specificity controls prothrombin activation.

puzzles.name: Flexible peptide linker
puzzles.blurb: The standard flexible linker for fusion proteins and single-chain antibodies. Glycine supplies backbone freedom and serine keeps the stretch soluble, so the two joined domains can move independently.

puzzles.name: Rigid helical linker
puzzles.blurb: Forms a stable alpha helix through salt bridges between the glutamate and lysine, holding two fused domains at a fixed distance. Used when a flexible linker would let the domains interact when they should not.
